01 · The foundation
A shard is one log, applied on three machines
the log
1041 New
1042 Cancel
1043 New
1044 Phase
1045 New
…
node a · leader
archive records → engine applies → book
node b · follower
archive records → engine applies → book
node c · follower
archive records → engine applies → book
What a shard is
One Aeron Cluster of three nodes hosting up to ten securities. Books never cross shards, so capacity grows by adding shards.
Why a replicated log
Replicate the inputs, not the state. Same log, same order, deterministic engine: same books on every node.
Why Aeron Cluster
Raft, sequencing, archive and snapshots in one library built for microseconds. Leader epochs rule out split-brain.
It replaced a hand-rolled primary and hot spare, which could double-publish after a bad failover.
02 · The rules
Four rules the whole design answers to
Determinism
Each shard is one thread over a Raft-replicated log, and every node must reach byte-identical state. A bad order is rejected, never thrown on — a throw would kill every node at the same log position.
No wall clock
Time comes from the consensus timestamp, never the machine it runs on. The one exception is metrics, and those histograms are write-only.
Zero allocation
The hot path allocates nothing, so no GC pause lands mid-match. Proven by two allocation tests and a soak under the no-op Epsilon collector.
Zero copy
Every message is encoded straight into Aeron's log buffer with tryClaim — never built in a scratch buffer and copied across.

One order, one cache line

8 × 8 bytes = exactly one 64-byte cache line, so touching an order costs one cache miss — the earlier struct-of-arrays layout cost up to seven.
1,000,000
orders per book, pre-allocated. Past the high-water mark an order is rejected — the pool never drains to a throw.
65,536
price levels per side, direct-mapped. An occupancy bitset finds the next best price 64 levels at a time.
≤ 10
securities per shard. Books never interact, so capacity scales by adding shards.
Prices and quantities are fixed-point int64 with 8 implied decimals — no floating point anywhere near matching.

Direct-mapped
level = (price − floor) ÷ tick. No tree, no search.
FIFO per level
Head and tail indices link orders by arrival: time priority, no allocation.
Occupancy bitset
One bit per level. The next best price is a leading-zero count — 64 levels a step.
Cancel by id
A primitive hash map from order id to pool slot.
The ladder is set wider than the static collar, so an out-of-band price is rejected long before it could overflow the ladder.

07 · Trading
The life of one order
1 · FIX adapter
A NewOrderSingle (35=D) arrives and is translated into an SBE NewOrder.
2 · Gateway
Checks security, participant and rights — a refusal happens here, before the log.
3 · Consensus
Raft gives the order a log position on a majority of nodes; the archive records it.
4 · Engine
Every node applies it identically: collars, self-match check, price-time matching.
5 · Report
The leader's report travels back: gateway, adapter, ExecutionReport (35=8).
At the same moment · leader only
Book event on shared memory → market-data → L1 · L2 · L3 on multicast → FIX market-data adapter → every participant's screen.
0.9–2%
of a 40–60 µs client round trip is spent in the gateway and engine. The rest is consensus, the archive write and the wire.
Round trip measured single-node on an Apple M4 Pro dev machine, JVM; FIX legs not included.
08 · The trading day
Each phase is a step on a path
CLOSED
Rejects orders. The resting book is kept.
PRE_OPEN
Accepts and books orders. No matching.
OPEN_AUCTION
Books orders and publishes an indicative price.
CONTINUOUS
Uncross once, then price-time matching.
Volatility halt: a fill breaches the dynamic collar
Opening auction
One uncrossing price that maximises executed volume.
Two collars
Static band rejects the order; dynamic band halts the book.
Self-match prevention
In continuous trading and in the auction.
Expiry
Date-based, purged while the market is closed.
09 · Market data
What participants see: the order book
AAPL's depth, rebuilt from the L2 feed by the same assembler every consumer uses.
L1 · L2 · L3
Best bid and offer, price levels, and every order — SBE on UDP multicast, written once for any audience.
Sequenced per shard
A subscriber spots a gap from the sequence number and resynchronises from the snapshot feed.
Slow readers only hurt themselves
The feed runs at the fastest receiver's pace, never the slowest.
A FIX market-data adapter consumes these same feeds and republishes them as FIX snapshots and incremental refreshes.
10 · Operating it
The control plane decides; nodes boot from files
Status — what the exchange is actually doing, read from the L3 feed. A halt shows up nowhere else.
Operations — phases, purge, snapshot, reopen. Audited as sent; confirmed by watching the feed.
Postgres-backed reference data is published as release files. The database is never on a boot path.
11 · When things fail
Losing a machine loses no orders
A node dies
The other two carry on. Raft elects a new leader whose engine is already in the same state, and its market-data starts publishing.
A gateway dies
It held no order state. Adapters reconnect to a peer, which reports correctly on orders it never saw.
The shard restarts
A snapshot bounds replay. The engine restores its books, then republishes each one to market data as an image.
A config change is unsafe
If new geometry would drop a resting order, the node refuses to start rather than come back quietly wrong.
No orchestrator on the core: Raft already fails over faster, and a rescheduled node would arrive with an empty archive.
12 · Measured
Matching is fast; the shared path sets the ceiling
0.42 µs
median cost of a whole new order inside the engine
~550k/s
aggregate ceiling across ten books, dedicated driver threads
0 bytes
allocated per order in steady state, proven three ways
463
tests, plus end-to-end, restart and soak scripts
Still open
The target is 1M orders/s per shard, ~1.8× above what was measured. The limit is the path every order shares — media driver, consensus, archive — not matching. What binds at ~550k/s is the next question.
Single node, Apple M4 Pro, JVM 21. Engine cost: one security, Serial GC. Ceiling: ten securities; ~350k/s with the default shared driver thread.
One thread, one log, every node the same.
Raft gives every node the same input; determinism guarantees the same output. Failover comes free.
Gateways and market-data hold no state of their own, so they can be replaced at will.
Formatting, fan-out and decisions each run in their own process, off the matching thread.
